claim: The British government sold 60 percent of Royal Mail in October 2013 at 330 pence a share, raising 1.98 billion pounds. The shares closed their first day at 455 pence — 38 percent above the sale price — and the National Audit Office, Parliament's public-spending auditor, found the 750 million pound first-day gain on the sold stake went to the new shareholders rather than the taxpayer. Royal Mail, the letter carrier, is the entity that was sold; Post Office Ltd, the branch counter network, was separated from it in 2012 and remains in public ownership.

sources.label: National Audit Office, "The privatisation of Royal Mail" (HC 1182, April 2014), executive summary
sources.quote: Royal Mail's share price rose to 455 pence (+38 per cent) on the first day of trading. The Department participated in the increase by retaining a 30 per cent stake, but the benefit of the price rise on the 60 per cent stake sold (a first day increase of £750 million) flowed to the new shareholders.

notes: Sourced from the NAO summary PDF, read with pdftotext (parliament.uk and commonslibrary.parliament.uk both 403 our fetcher). Written to correct a conflation the surfacing clip makes: the UK 'post office' that was privatised is Royal Mail; Post Office Ltd — the branch network of Horizon-scandal fame — was demerged in 2012 and is still state-owned, so a complaint about post-office counters is not a complaint about the 2013 sale. Service quality after privatisation is a separate, contested question and is not asserted here.
